questions.prompt: Hicks’s opening claim about why we should bother with logic’s hard abstractions is that, for human beings, logic is:
choices: A An optional hobby useful only to professional mathematicians.
B The most practical thing one can master.
C A purely ornamental tradition inherited from medieval monks.
D A substitute for using the body well in survival.
questions.explain: He starts by asking why bother, then claims logic is the most practical thing humans can master—controversial even among pro-logic people.

questions.prompt: What does Hicks say Aristotle’s logical writings are collectively called, and what does that Greek word mean?
choices: A The Republic; it means a city.
B The Organon; it means a tool.
C The Categories only; it means a list of insults.
D The Symposium; it means a feast.
questions.explain: Aristotle’s logic books are the Organon—Greek for a tool: tools of thinking for different circumstances.

questions.prompt: On Hicks’s reading of Aristotle’s formulation, the principle of non-contradiction says that:
choices: A The same attribute cannot at the same time belong and not belong to the same subject in the same respect.
B Contradictions are allowed if they are emotionally sincere.
C Every dispute has two equally true sides.
D Reality regularly contradicts itself, so thought should too.
questions.explain: He quotes Metaphysics: the same attribute cannot belong and not belong to the same subject at the same time in the same respect.

questions.prompt: In this course’s technical use, an argument is:
choices: A Two people yelling insults at each other.
B A structure of propositions with a conclusion and premise(s) offered as reasons for it.
C Any emotionally intense speech, whether or not reasons are given.
D A list of facts with no inferred claim.
questions.explain: Yelling is not an argument. An argument has a conclusion (what to believe) and premises (why).

questions.prompt: How does Hicks distinguish truth from validity when evaluating an argument?
choices: A Truth is whether the pieces correspond to reality; validity is whether the inference’s form preserves that support.
B Validity means the premises are popular; truth means they are Latin.
C They are synonyms—both just mean “sounds right.”
D Truth applies only to conclusions; validity applies only to insults.
questions.explain: Truth: do the components match reality? Validity: is the structure of the inference good, independent of those contents?
